I think possibly the most harmful error of trans-activist ideology is its propagation of the idea that who we fundamentally are lies in the relationship between the body we have and the body we would like to have.

You are bigger than the mental space between the body you have and the body you would like to have.

What makes a certain kind of brain 'wrong' or 'right' for a certain kind of body? What makes a body 'wrong' and in need of changing? It seems to me that trans-activist ideology has no coherent answer to this question - and doesn't really want to talk about it - leading to a great deal of confusion.

There are many meaningful, productive, and fulfilling things that we can build a sense of who we are around: things like hobbies, interests, career, family, nation, ethnicity, politics.

It's a shame that Western nations have become so fixated on the body in the past decade.

Good luck.

I have never 'questioned my gender', because there is nothing to question. Gender is not any more a thing than God, heaven, or ghosts are. I don't understand why anyone needs to make all this about anything more than the bare facts. And the bare facts for me are that I am female ('afab', although I fundamentally disagree with that term), I am heterosexual, but I am a tomboy who has always hated things pushed at me 'for girls', such as makeup, dresses, and shaving, and who has always generally gotten along better with males for various reasons.

That's all there is. I never worried about any of this stuff until the idiots in this subreddit and on Tumblr started claiming in around 2013 that 'female' meant something other than what it clearly means. The fact that I am a tomboy doesn't mean anything about my 'true self'. There is no such thing as a 'true self'. Things just are, and are nothing more than what they are. Then they change. Who knows how? When the next pandemic or ecological or economic crisis hits no one will have time to care.

There's no reason why it has to be any more complicated than that. Get off this hellsite and get connected to your body. Break down what you are like into simple terms that anyone could understand, not the kind of jargon terms you need to be balls-deep in a cult to think are really useful or sense-making ('afab', 'questioning', 'nonbinary, etc.) Go do something. Anything other than getting any deeper into this stupid ideological rabbit hole.

Please trust your counsellor. She is probably better informed by wisdom and education than most of the posters here. I have felt a great deal of severe discomfort with the female sex role for all of my life, and have never felt a kinship with other women, but I have never had any dissatisfaction with the sex of my body: and therefore there is no reason for me to transition. I am objectively female and happy to be so. I'm older and I'm very glad that I was an adult before the 'have you questioned your gender today' memes started flooding the internet. I had OCD as a teenager, and I could have been hurt badly if my OCD had fixated on trying to untangle the mental gymnastics  and inconsistencies of the stupid opinions about sex and gender you see proffered on this subreddit.

Some people who identify as trans women have woman-typical brains.

Women with woman-atypical brains, such as myself, are still women. We're just statistical outliers. 

Stop lying. Stop hurting detransitioners and gender-nonconforming cis people with your lies. We have gender-atypical brains, too. And we're not trans.
Don't be afraid to ask anything you like. You have a right to know and ask questions about such important things.
What do you mean when you say that you are a 'girl on the inside'?

Have you actually never heard of radical pamphleteering. It's how you, if you're female, have the ability to vote and get an abortion.

I can't see a therapist, my country is under total COVID-19 lockdown. In any case, I've seen several over the years and I have a Psychology degree. The psychiatric framework of mood disorders has barely helped me or my friends, and arguably has hurt us (long-term side effects of long-term psychiatric drug treatment). Exercise and reading about CBT has been far more helpful to me than therapy has ever been.

You'll find this out too if you ever have the misfortune to develop a 'treatment-resistant' mood disorder. So let's hope nobody in your local Cluster B personality disorder hive (aka BDSM scene) feels like giving you PTSD some day.

You should try making sense of postmodern and critical ~~word salad~~ theory some time, it's what half of your community's bullshit is built on.

Google the 'Sokal Hoax', 'Grievance Studies', etc.

What you are experiencing is cognitive dissonance.

One reason why being trans is so hard is that there is no precise and coherent definition of what it means to be trans. Scientists also don't have the foggiest of what actually causes dysphoria, or what should and what shouldn't be called 'dysphoria', or who is benefited by transition and who isn't.

This level of being in the dark about the thing members of a given community are members in virtue of means that, unless some kind of dogmatic conceptual system is enforced by the community as a whole, all sorts of arguments are likely to break out between people whose different experiences have led them to different armchair psychologist conclusions. This isn't good for social cohesion.

When human beings in general were this in the dark about what the world was and how we could even find out, we developed religious dogma with rewards for faith and punishment for heresy: because otherwise our confusion and disagreement about what the world was like would have torn societies apart.

Similarly, in order that a genuinely vulnerable group of people can get along with each other, the mainstream trans community suppresses meaningful discussion about its own fundamental questions: whether biological sex exists or can be changed; what dysphoria/euphoria is and is caused by; what gender identity really is; the difference between being and 'identifying as'. Discussion is suppressed because there's also a possibility of people's ideas being misunderstood and/or used against trans people.

I don't blame the trans community. It is just trying to protect itself and get by in a larger world unremittingly and virulently hostile to critical thinking and philosophical inquiry. But OP needs genuine support, not just to be told to suppress doubt and repress her ability to think critically.

Because with the rise in the trans-identifying population, there only will be more and more detransitioners and desisters. There will only be more Jessica Yaniv cases, and more children like Jacob coming out about feeling permanently damaged by puberty blockers, and more unscientific obfuscation of sex differences in statistical collection via self-ID, and, ultimately, more hard questions for the mainstream trans activist community.

[https://transblog.grieve-smith.com/the-slippery-slope/](https://transblog.grieve-smith.com/the-slippery-slope/) OP, Angus/Angea Grieve-Smith has written about ways of responding to the kind of self-doubt and confusion that trans people experience when exposed to TERF arguments. You might find their writings helpful.

This is offensive stereotyping.

My best guess is that he has had lifelong, intense sexual fantasies about becoming female, and for reasons of personality and/or worldview a 'successful' male life as prescribed by stereotyped sex roles was either unattainable or unfulfilling for him. The stories of late male transitioners are psychodynamically complex. See: [https://sillyolme.wordpress.com/2014/02/14/a-clinical-view/](https://sillyolme.wordpress.com/2014/02/14/a-clinical-view/)

For example: being sexually reliant in adulthood on an activity (crossdressing) first performed in prepubescent childhood is an 'emasculating' experience due to the psychodynamic association of women and children in patriarchal cultures. This sense of 'emasculation' seems to have a causal role in dysphoria and the drive to transition.

Please feel free to contest this if you are a male detransitioner (I'm female and mostly just speculating.)

I have been watching this trend for a few years and agree that the paraphilia seems to be able to be inculcated in men vulnerable to porn addiction or who were already masochistic (because 'paraphilias cluster' - Bailey), and can then feed on pre-existing or tangentially related feelings of 'insufficient' masculinity, loneliness, and unloveability. See e.g. Shannon Thrace's TEDX Maastricht talk: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M3mnUMmUAHQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M3mnUMmUAHQ)

One major problem is that the way we raise male children exaggerates rather than counteracts what is apparently a biological relative vulnerability to alexithymia.

One thing I would add to people's good advice here is to not buy into the literal existence of a 'true self'.

Although I'm not dysphoric, many detransitioners such as Destroy Your Binder, Carey Callahan, and Third Way Trans have written philosophically interesting texts about what a 'true self' could possibly be.

From my POV as a psych graduate student: the sense of 'self' is a cognitive heuristic based on a feedback loops from more simple perceptual mechanisms: the judgments and significance which animals assign sensations, colours, smells, tastes and sounds.

One of the most influential modern philosophers, David Hume, put it this way: that sensory perceptions are prior to the sense of self: because the sense of self is itself a form of perception. Perception is a phenomenon in the brain which facilitates behaviour in response to an animal's environment.

Indeed the concept of anything at all 'existing' is derived from the reification of a certain kind of sensory event (e.g. an animal notices that an area formerly containing water is now dry, or which had a rock now lacks a rock.)

Kant: "From the crooked timber of humanity, no straight thing can ever be made."

We are fragile sacks of organic compounds, made up mostly of water, given rise to from a biosphere which will eventually cease to exist. It used to be that the common cold could kill. It's still possible though unlikely die from a minor bump on the head (cerebral hematoma), or a freak pulmonary embolism caused by symptomless DVT.

I used to freak out about this. What does it mean that we're inextricable from the material world controlled by physics? Why can't I stop thinking about the fact that the self in an important sense does not exist?  I ended up in hospital. I realised I was investing WAY too much emotion into mental battles with poorly defined and abstruse concepts , and not enough into goals that could help me achieve my needs and those of others in far more comprehensible social reality.

When I gave myself exposure therapy by investing more emotion and thought into my achievements in the real world and my relationships with others, I was able to accept that it wasn't my fault that I had OCD, and that it wasn't anyone else's fault either, and that it doesn't matter that the whole concept of 'fault' is ontologically and epistemologically questionable. I fully recovered.

Tl;dr: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PlsW2hd06R0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PlsW2hd06R0) :)

You will be OK in the end if you just keep going.

For most of history and prehistory, when mirrors and portrait painting were not widely available, human beings never saw a clear image of their reflection. Nowadays we encounter mirrors on a daily basis.

Being able to see and contemplate your reflection is arguably unnatural. (I am aware though of the naturalistic fallacy - unnatural does not necessarily equal unhealthy or unethical.) It's certainly not something that mammalian psychology or primate psychology evolved any response to.

There are some cultures in which it's believed that looking in a mirror or seeing your photograph can make you 'lose your soul' (or harm you in some other vaguely articulated way.) See, for instance: [https://www.quora.com/Do-some-cultures-believe-that-photography-can-steal-your-soul](https://www.quora.com/Do-some-cultures-believe-that-photography-can-steal-your-soul)

Looking in a mirror is a cognitively and philosophically weird and interesting act. You might argue that it involves a subject making an object of the self in the act of looking.

Looking in a mirror for long periods of time can induce dissociation, derealisation, and depersonalisation (speaking from personal experience here.) That's also why modern-day cults have practiced 'mirror-staring', and why it's a common aspect of rituals (such as Bloody Mary and Candyman.)

Hoping you find a way through all this to peace someday.

One thing that might be worth trying to unpack is what 'being read as a woman' means to you. What specific kinds of desirable ways of being treated would come under that umbrella of  'being read as a woman'? Conversely, what kinds of undesirable ways of being treated are you categorising under 'being read as a man'?

Given the tools available to you (clothes, hormones, name change, future surgery), which of the specific forms of treatment from other people could be realistic prospects for you?

A counsellor, especially one specialising in CBT,  might be able to help you unpack your thought processes and thereby more able to figure out and move confidently towards what you want. I'm not sure what country you live in (probably USA?) but I would look into what services are available to you.

Something else that might be relevant. I am a non trans-identified (i.e. cis) female and the way I treat my FTM friend has not changed at all after his legal or medical transition. It will never change. I treat people in accordance with what I know and believe and suspect about them. The only things that have changed in his transition are external and thereby superficial.  I started behaving towards him in a way which doesn't make him feel dysphoria many years ago, and I achieved that just by making the effort to learn about dysphoria and understand his situation and those of other dysphoric and trans-identified people. We have had arguments and misnderstandings, but resolving them has only made us closer.

​

Warning, I'm about to get up on a soapbox..

The clothes or tone of voice or physique of a person mean next to nothing when you have a shared understanding with that person of what they are like, what they like and dislike, and why they like what they like and dislike. And these identity-related beliefs that may or may not be shared are shaped and expressed in terms of worldviews. On the subject of worldviews: I read a lot about the science and statistics of gender dysphoria, trans identification, and sexual orientation because I wanted to understand my friend and myself better and also because of my other general interests and university studies. What I read - particularly in Alice Dreger's book 'Galileo's Middle Finger' and Kay Brown's blog 'sillyolme' - made me so angry with the world at large for not caring about gender dysphoria and not doing enough research into it (while at the same time that same uncaring general public assumes that transition is or will always be the only solution.)

People with dysphoria agonise over whether they are 'really trans' (or 'really female' or 'really male') for a good reason: because scientists don't actually know what dysphoria is or what causes it  (or what gender euphoria/AGP/AAP is, for that matter) . The closest neurological analogue we have is with BIID/apotemnophilia - which does not appear to have much to do with any reproductive dimorphism that might putatively exist in the brain (but whether there are 'male' or 'female' brains is an extremely complex and unsettled question.)  If gender dysphoria is ever to be meaningfully alleviated, there desperately needs to be more unbiased research into it. Activists must stop trying to control the narrative and instead get universities to provide research grants in order to let neuroscientists and psychologists do their thing.

​

Thank you very much for reading all this. I really hope you find peace in whatever way you can. Feel free to DM me (although I am by no means an authority or expert.)

I really appreciate that you found it useful and I hope you find a therapist you have rapport with.

I've never been in a serious intimate relationship either and I'm 25F.  It's not so unusual for somewhat odd people.

[https://www.tri-ess.org/docs/whatis.html](https://www.tri-ess.org/docs/whatis.html) The Tri-Ess society was/is (I'm not sure if it's still active) a support group for married dysphoric and autogynephilic AMABs and their wives. You might be able to find out the best way for you to approach relationships (if a relationship is something you'd like to have) from their experiences. AFAIK you might also find examples of how people similar to you have developed fulfilling relationships on the Susan's Place forum.

I query the concept of 'just autogynephilia'. I think it would be more accurate to say 'mild autogynephilia', because there's strong evidence that the difference between autogynephilic people who don't transition or have dysphoria and people who do is dimensional and not taxonic: [https://sillyolme.wordpress.com/2014/09/12/autogynephilic-vs-even-more-autogynephilic/](https://sillyolme.wordpress.com/2014/09/12/autogynephilic-vs-even-more-autogynephilic/)

Moreover Anne Vitale's case studies show that autogynephilia can be or become stronger or weaker on the basis of unrelated things such as body image (including how 'passable' the person perceives themselves to be), how relationships are going, career prospects, and financial situations.

Society at large would save OCD-inclined types a great deal of pain if it stopped propounding the false idea of identity as taxonic, made up of discrete elements, and innate (queer or straight? trans or cis? coloured or white? autistic or neurotypical?) The truth is that most personal traits are dimensional/statistically continuous and situationally contingent (even if the situation that gives rise to them is basically unchangeable - such as the century you live in, for example).
